LAION TTS annotated speech corpus — statistical profile

Distribution statistics for every annotation field, vocal-burst statistics, and a mined catalogue of emotional and vocal trajectories. Measured on 130,785,282 annotated utterances across 16,421 index shards and 8 source datasets.
Built 2026-08-19 on JUPITER. Nothing on this page has been checked by ear; every number is a statistic over model-produced annotations.

Read this first if you read nothing else This document profiles a very large collection of short speech recordings that have been automatically labelled with emotion scores, voice-quality scores and markers for non-word sounds like laughs and sighs. Three things it establishes:
  1. The corpus is 130,785,282 utterances, not the ~135.8 M that was estimated from shard counts. That estimate assumed a uniform ~8,510 rows per shard; the measured average is 7,965 over the 16,421 shards actually read. Everything below is counted, not extrapolated.
  2. Most emotion scores are extremely concentrated near zero. For emo_Anger, 34 % of the entire corpus falls in a single histogram bin a few thousandths of a point wide. Decile buckets below the median therefore do not exist as distinct value ranges — a fact that silently breaks any analysis that assumes emotion scores are spread out, and that we report explicitly rather than smoothing over.
  3. Smooth emotional trajectories are abundant but the step cap decides everything. Loosening the per-step cap from 0.10 to 0.25 changes the number of qualifying emotion trajectories by roughly three orders of magnitude. Some combinations that were requested are arithmetically impossible and correctly return zero.

1 · What this corpus is

The corpus is a pile of short speech recordings gathered from 8 different sources — podcasts, European parliamentary video, audiobooks, volunteer-read sentences, German read speech and several internal collections — and then run through a set of machine-learning annotators that listen to each recording and emit numbers describing it.

Three words are used constantly below, so they are defined here.

  • Utterance. One short stretch of speech by (usually) one person, typically a sentence or a phrase. It is the unit of everything on this page: one utterance = one row of data. Median length is 8.5 s.
  • Shard. A storage file holding a few thousand utterances' worth of annotations, in Apache Parquet format. The corpus is split into 16,421 shards purely so that it can be written and read in parallel; shards carry no meaning. We stream them one at a time because the whole table — 130,785,282 rows by about 230 columns — does not fit in memory.
  • Dataset. The original source a shard came from (podcast, emolia, eurospeech, snippets, commonvoice, evasnippets, mls, kartoffelphon). Sources differ enormously in recording conditions and speaking style, which is why almost every table below is broken down by dataset.

What is it for? Mainly training text-to-speech and voice-conversion models that can be directed — told to sound angry, or tired, or to chuckle mid-sentence — rather than only reading text flatly. To train such a model you need many examples labelled with how they actually sound, and you need to know which labels are plentiful and which are almost absent. That is what Part 1 measures. Part 3 goes further and looks for examples of a voice changing over consecutive clips, which is what you need if you want a model that can perform a gradual emotional shift instead of a fixed mood.

2 · What each annotation field means

Every utterance carries about 230 columns. This document profiles the 105 numeric ones. They come from three different annotator models.

The 40 emotion scores (emo_*)

Produced by Empathic Insight, a model that listens to a clip and outputs one intensity number per emotion, on a nominal 0–7 scale (0 = the emotion is absent, 7 = extremely strong). The 40 emotions are not mutually exclusive: a clip can be simultaneously amused and impatient. Because it is a regression model, it can emit slightly negative values; these occur on every dimension and are kept as measured rather than clipped.

The 57 VoiceNet dimensions (vn_*_reg)

Produced by VoiceNet, which scores how the voice sounds rather than what it feels: tempo, brightness, breathiness, perceived age, whether the delivery sounds like newsreading or like a casual chat, and so on. Each is a continuous regression (the _reg suffix) that in practice also behaves like a 0–7 scale. There is a parallel set of vn_*_bucket columns holding the same judgement discretised into integer bins; those are not profiled here, because averaging or z-scoring a bucket index is meaningless.

Judgement fields

  • genuineness_0_6 (0–6) — does the emotion sound felt, or performed/read? Low = flat or acted, high = spontaneous.
  • blend_0_10 (0–10) — how much several emotions are mixed in the same clip rather than one clean emotion.
  • qual_* (four fields) — recording quality, speech quality, background cleanliness, and how enjoyable the content is.
  • dur_s, n_words — duration in seconds and transcript word count.

Vocal bursts

A vocal burst is a non-word vocal sound: a chuckle, a gasp, a sigh, a throat-clear, a groan. They carry a lot of emotional information and are exactly what flat TTS cannot do, so the corpus marks them. Each utterance has n_bursts (how many burst events occurred) and burst_labels (which classes of burst occurred). Part 2 profiles them and explains an important subtlety about those two fields.

Three caveats — read before quoting a number
  • EuroSpeech is very nearly but not quite complete. 2,746 shards were read; roughly 25 more were still being written when this pass ran. Every EuroSpeech row below is therefore a very tight lower bound. EuroSpeech is 7.0 % of rows, so the pooled figures will drift by well under a tenth of a percent when it lands.
  • KartoffelPhon is included in Parts 1 and 2 but excluded from Part 3. It arrived late, after this analysis had started, and was re-read specially: 218 shards, 2,616,656 utterances, almost entirely German. Its distribution and burst statistics are fully valid and are included everywhere in Parts 1–2. But it has no speaker labels yet — the job that produces them failed on a library incompatibility and is being fixed — and a trajectory is meaningless without knowing which clips share a speaker. It is therefore excluded from Part 3 entirely. That is "not measurable yet", not "zero".
  • The corpus grew underneath this analysis. It stood at 15,957 index shards when the pass began and 16,421 by the time the report was written. The table above is the authoritative record of what was actually read; it is the set every number refers to.

Measured vs. extrapolated. Every count in this document is an exact count over the shard set above, with two clearly-flagged exceptions: (a) percentiles are read off fixed-edge histograms with 4096 bins, so they carry an error below one bin width (minimum and maximum are exact, tracked separately); (b) the language mix of mined trajectories in Part 3 is re-weighted from a capped sample and is labelled as estimated wherever it appears. Nothing else is extrapolated.

Numerical method. Means and standard deviations over 130,785,282 values were accumulated in float64 as (n, mean, M2) triples merged pairwise with Chan's formula, never as a running ∑x², which at this scale loses precision badly and can produce a negative variance.

4 · Statistics primer

Two ideas are used throughout. If you already know them, skip to Part 1.

Z-score. The 40 emotions and 57 voice dimensions are on different scales: a typical emo_Interest is around 1.9 while a typical emo_Pain is around 0.01, so "1.0" means something completely different on the two. A z-score removes that by restating a value as how many standard deviations it sits from the average:

z = (x − mean) / standard deviation

z = 0 is exactly average, z = +2 is well above average, z = −1 is somewhat below. Because it is unitless, a z-score of +2 on Anger is directly comparable to +2 on Tempo. The mean and standard deviation used here are always the global ones (all datasets, all languages pooled) so that a dataset's z-score says how that dataset differs from the corpus, not from itself.

Decile. Sort every utterance by one field and cut the sorted list into ten equal-sized groups. The first group is the lowest-scoring 10 %, the tenth is the highest-scoring 10 %. The nine cut points are the decile edges; the tenth group is the "top decile". A percentile is the same idea with 100 groups — p90 is the value below which 90 % of the corpus falls.

The cut points here are computed once on the whole corpus and then reused for every dataset and language. That is deliberate: if each dataset got its own deciles, every dataset would trivially have 10 % of its rows in each of its own buckets and the tables would say nothing. With global cut points, a dataset with 31 % of its rows in the top global decile of Anger is telling you it is genuinely angrier than the corpus.

Why a z-score is often the wrong tool here A z-score is only a good summary when the distribution is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped. Most emotion fields in this corpus are nothing like that: they are strongly right-skewed with a huge spike at zero and a long thin tail. On such a shape, z = +2 is not near the 98th percentile — for emo_Anger, z > +2 covers 5.4 % of the corpus, not 2.3 %. Wherever this happens, prefer the percentile columns. Both are reported side by side for exactly this reason, and both are stored in norm_stats.json.

5.2 The zero-inflation problem — and what it does to deciles

This is the single most important structural fact about the emotion annotations, and it changes how every table after it must be read.

Most emotions are absent from most clips, and the annotator does not express absence as a spread of small values — it collapses them onto almost the same number. Concretely, we histogrammed each field into 4096 bins spanning its robust range and asked what share of the corpus lands in the single most populated bin:

For emo_Anger, 33.5 % of all 130,785,282 utterances share one bin about 0.00038 points wide. The consequence is unavoidable arithmetic: if a third of the corpus has effectively the same value, you cannot cut that third into distinct deciles. The decile edges are still nine different numbers, but several of them differ only in the fourth decimal place and enclose no data at all.

How we handled it, and why it matters Decile bucket counts here are computed by assigning each histogram bin whole to the bucket its centre falls in. The obvious alternative — interpolating within the bin — would invent a smooth ramp across several buckets that does not exist in the data, and would have reported a tidy 10 % per bucket that was pure fiction. With whole-bin assignment the counts still sum exactly to n, and a tied decile shows up honestly as an empty bucket. When you see a 0 in a decile table below, it means "no utterance falls between these two cut points because the cut points are essentially the same number", not "missing data".

The practical advice: for the concentrated emotions, do not threshold on a z-score or on a low decile. The only well-separated part of those distributions is the upper tail, so use p90/p99 or the top-decile counts in 5.4. Fields like emo_Interest, emo_Concentration, all 57 VoiceNet dimensions, genuineness_0_6, blend_0_10 and dur_s are well spread and behave normally — their decile tables show a clean 10 % per bucket.

5.3 Decile buckets, with counts

Cut points come from the whole corpus. Each row shows how many of that scope's utterances fall in each global decile bucket — D1 is the corpus's lowest-scoring tenth, D10 the highest. For the pooled corpus every well-behaved field reads 10 % across; deviations from 10 % are the concentration effect of 5.2. For a single dataset or language, deviation from 10 % is the real signal: it says that group is high or low on that field relative to the corpus.

Tables are collapsed by default — there are 105 fields × 24 scopes. Cut-point values themselves are in the first table.

5.4 How often extremes occur

Two explicit, consistently-applied definitions:

  • Extreme-high (decile): the value is at or above the corpus's p90 for that field — i.e. it is in the top global decile. Likewise extreme-low is at or below p10. By construction the whole corpus has 10 % in each; a dataset having more than 10 % means it is over-represented there.
  • Extreme (|z| > 2): the value is more than two global standard deviations from the global mean. On a bell curve this would be 4.6 % of data; on these skewed fields it is not, and the difference between the two definitions is itself informative.

Counts are numbers of utterances. "% of scope" is relative to the rows that scope contributes.

5.5 Language splits

The 16 languages with at least 5,000 utterances, pooled across datasets. Interpretation is the same as above: the number is the share of that language's utterances in the corpus-wide top decile, so 10 % is neutral.

Confounded, on purpose Language and dataset are heavily entangled here — Danish is almost entirely EuroSpeech, Chinese almost entirely emolia. A language difference in these tables is therefore not evidence about the language; it is mostly evidence about which source it came from and how that source was recorded. The per-dataset×language cells in norm_stats.json let you disentangle the two where both have enough rows.

5.6 Genuineness in detail

genuineness_0_6 asks whether the emotion in a clip sounds felt or performed, on a 0–6 scale. It was singled out for a full breakdown. It is one of the well-behaved fields — only 5.7 % of the corpus sits in its modal bin — so deciles and z-scores are both meaningful for it.

Corpus-wide: mean 2.524, std 1.646, median 2.574, range 0.000 to 6.000. Decile cut points: 0.208, 0.760, 1.357, 1.982, 2.574, 3.109, 3.611, 4.120, 4.719.

Read a row as: of this group's utterances, what percentage lands in each corpus-wide genuineness decile. A group with a big number under % D10 sounds more spontaneous than the corpus average; a group loaded on % D1 sounds flatter or more read.

6 · Part 2 — Vocal bursts

A vocal burst is a sound the voice makes that is not a word: a chuckle, a gasp, a sigh, a groan, a throat-clear. They matter because they are the clearest signal of spontaneous emotion in speech and because synthetic voices are conspicuously bad at them, so a corpus's burst inventory largely determines whether a model trained on it can laugh convincingly.

Critical subtlety: two fields, two different quantities The index has both n_bursts and burst_labels, and they do not agree — corpus-wide n_bursts sums to 63,249,675 while burst_labels contains only 46,155,884 entries. We checked this directly against the raw data: for every utterance, burst_labels holds the set of distinct burst classes present (its length always equals its number of unique values), while n_bursts counts burst events, including repeats of the same class. An utterance with three chuckles and one throat-clear has n_bursts = 4 and burst_labels = ["Chuckle", "Ahem"].

So the per-class tables below count utterances containing at least one burst of that class, which is the only thing the data supports. They are not event counts, and they do not sum to 63,249,675. Total events are only available in aggregate, and are reported as such.

7 · Part 3 — Trajectory mining

7.1 What a trajectory is, and why anyone wants one

Everything so far treats each utterance as an isolated point. A trajectory treats a sequence of them: two to five consecutive clips of the same voice, in the order they were spoken, chosen so that some quality of the voice moves substantially and smoothly from the first clip to the last.

Concretely: the same person's voice starting calm in clip 1, a little tenser in clip 2, clearly irritated by clip 3, and angry by clip 5. Played back end-to-end that is a short performance with an emotional arc.

Why this is worth mining. A text-to-speech model trained only on isolated clips learns to produce a fixed mood per utterance: you can ask it for "angry" and get angry, but you cannot ask it to become angry over a paragraph, because it has never seen an example of becoming. Chains like these are the training material for directable, gradually-shifting delivery. They are also the only honest way to test whether the emotion annotations are coherent over time for one speaker rather than noise sampled fresh for each clip.

The mining is entirely procedural — every chain in the corpus that satisfies the stated numeric rules is counted. Nothing was hand-picked, and no example was chosen because it sounded good.

7.2 What counts as "the same speaker" in each dataset

A trajectory is only meaningful if all its clips are the same voice. The index does not carry a speaker column, so the speaker had to be recovered from the structure of the uid. This differs per dataset and it is the single biggest caveat in Part 3.

datasetspeaker basisrows usedtracksadjacent pairs… of which contiguous% with real timestampshow the speaker was recovered
podcastproxy26,606,892330,57126,276,32130.0uid = <episode>_<offset>. An episode is usually a multi-speaker conversation, so a track is a recording, not a person.
emoliadataset-provided81,824,5812,986,54978,838,03272,431,2620.0uid = <lang>_<speaker>_W<window>; the speaker field of the source equals the uid minus the window suffix. For the YODAS portion a ‘speaker’ is one source video, so a multi-speaker video is pooled.
eurospeechproxy7,706,04616,0727,689,9746,313,300100.0uid = <country>_<video>_<start_ms>_<end_ms>. A video is a whole parliamentary sitting with many speakers, so the track alone is not a speaker. Only the contiguous-run restriction makes it approximately one; unrestricted EuroSpeech numbers are upper bounds.
snippetsproxy2,633,03747,2872,585,7502,5740.0uid = <chunk>_<offset>; a chunk is a slice of one source recording, usually but not provably one speaker.
commonvoicenoneexcluded————uid is an opaque hash, the true speaker id exists only in the source metadata, and the clips are independent read sentences with no temporal relation. Excluded from Part 3 entirely.
evasnippetsproxy500,007195,747304,26010.0emotion-bucketed reference snippets; almost every chunk has a single member, so there is very little to chain.
mlsexact431,3388,180423,158389,138100.0uid = <speaker>_<chapter>_<utt>. The speaker id is the LibriVox reader — one real human per id. Timing came from a side table built from the source metadata.
kartoffelphonnoneexcluded————speaker / pseudo-speaker labels have not been produced yet (the embedding job failed on a library incompatibility and is being repaired). Without them there is no way to know which clips share a voice. Excluded from Part 3 entirely, but fully included in Parts 1 and 2.
Only MLS gives a real human speaker id Everywhere else "same speaker" means "same recording", which for podcasts and parliament means possibly a different person from clip to clip. MLS is the only dataset whose trajectory counts can be read as “one person changing” without qualification — and it is 0.33 % of the corpus. The large numbers below come from proxy speakers and must be read as “chains within one recording”. They are still directly useful for training (a single recording is usually a single voice), but they are an upper bound on true single-speaker chains.

KartoffelPhon pseudo-speaker labels never landed, so it contributes nothing here; there is no KartoffelPhon row and no estimate for one.

7.3 Putting 97 different scales into [0,1]

Emotions and voice dimensions are on incomparable scales, so before any threshold like “moved by 0.25” can mean anything, each dimension has to be mapped to a common 0–1 range. Two schemes are reported so you can see how much the choice matters.

  • ecdfm — tie-aware rank. A value becomes its position in the whole corpus: 0 = lowest-scoring clip, 1 = highest. “Moved 0.25” then means “crossed a quarter of the corpus”, which is the same statement on every dimension. Fitted on the exact global histograms of all 130,785,282 rows.
  • p1p99 — robust linear rescale. (x − p1) / (p99 − p1), clipped to [0,1]. Keeps the original shape, so “moved 0.25” means “a quarter of the field's robust range”. On the zero-inflated emotions this leaves most clips bunched near 0.
A defect we found and fixed — worth knowing if you reuse this code The first version of the rank normaliser built a 2,001-point quantile ladder from a 5.9 M-row sample and evaluated it with np.interp. On these distributions that is broken: emo_Awe's ladder has only 120 distinct values out of 2,001 because ~94 % of the ladder is the single number 0.0000. Interpolating a query that equals a repeated knot lands at the top of the tied block, so essentially every clip was assigned Awe ≈ 0.94 and Awe came out as the strongest emotion of 23 % of all clips — an artefact of the interpolator, not a property of the corpus, and it was steering the whole peak-emotion rule.

The fix is the textbook treatment of ties, the mid-rank: u = (#{X < x} + ½ #{X = x}) / n, which sends a tied block to the middle of the ranks it occupies instead of the top. After the fix the strongest-emotion distribution is spread sensibly across many emotions. All Part 3 numbers below use the fixed normaliser.

7.4 The rules, stated exactly

A chain of k clips (2 ≤ k ≤ 5) of one track, in time order, qualifies on a dimension when:

  1. Total change ≥ T, where T is 0.25 (the base tier) or 0.50 (the strong tier), measured as |value at last clip − value at first clip| in the [0,1] space.
  2. Every single step ≤ C, the per-step cap, swept at 0.10 / 0.20 / 0.25. This is what forces a ramp instead of a jump: reaching 0.25 through four small steps is the thing we want; a single 0.25 lurch is not.
  3. The dimension is relevant, which rejects flat chains. Two rules are reported:
    • Rule A (endpoints) — the moving dimension must be the strongest emotion of the first clip or of the last clip. This is the strict reading and it rejects flatness by construction: if the same emotion peaks at both ends, that emotion must itself have moved by ≥ T for the chain to count. Rule A is the headline.
    • Rule B (any dimension) — any of the 40 emotions may be the one that moves. Reported as a permissive upper bound only.
    VoiceNet space uses Rule B only: "the peak VoiceNet dimension" is meaningless because the 57 regressions are independent scales, not competing categories.
  4. Link mode: any = consecutive in time within the track, whatever the gap; contig = additionally genuinely adjacent in the source recording (gap ≤ 2 s where real timestamps exist, consecutive ordinal otherwise).
What the thresholds mean for the audio you would get T = 0.25 is a clear but ordinary shift — the voice crosses a quarter of the corpus on that dimension, e.g. from typically-calm to noticeably-annoyed. T = 0.50 is a dramatic arc across half the corpus, and is much rarer. The per-step cap controls how the change is delivered: at C = 0.25 the whole shift may happen in one cut between two clips, which tends to sound like an edit; at C = 0.10 no single seam may move more than a tenth of the corpus, so the change has to be spread over several clips and sounds like a ramp. Lower cap = smoother and much rarer.
Some requested grid cells are arithmetically impossible — and correctly return zero With a cap C and k clips there are k−1 steps, so the largest reachable total change is (k−1)×C. Therefore: T = 0.25 with C = 0.10 needs k ≥ 4; T = 0.25 with C = 0.20 needs k ≥ 3; T = 0.50 with C = 0.20 needs k ≥ 4; and T = 0.50 with C = 0.10 needs 6 clips, which exceeds the 5-clip limit and is therefore empty everywhere. A zero in those cells is arithmetic, not absence of data.

The same reasoning explains why the k = 2 column is essentially zero everywhere in the length tables below. A 2-clip chain has exactly one step, so its total change is its step size; requiring “total ≥ T and step ≤ C” is satisfiable only when C ≥ T, and then only by chains sitting exactly on the boundary. At T = C = 0.25 that yields 4 chains in the entire corpus. This is the requirement working as intended: a two-clip cut is precisely the abrupt jump the per-step cap exists to exclude. Every useful trajectory here is 3 to 5 clips long.

VoiceNet trajectories are far more abundant than emotion trajectories — roughly two orders of magnitude more at the same thresholds. Two reasons: Rule B applies (any of 57 dimensions may be the one that moves, versus Rule A's restriction to the peak emotion), and voice qualities like tempo, loudness and brightness genuinely drift continuously through a recording in a way that categorical emotion does not.

7.9 The output file

Mined trajectories are written as Parquet with one row per chain:

dataset      source dataset
space        "emo" or "vn"
k            number of clips in the chain (2-5)
speaker      speaker / track identity held constant (see 7.2)
track        the recording the chain came from
lang         language tag
dim          WHICH dimension moves, e.g. emo_Anger or vn_TEMP_reg
start,end    that dimension's normalised value at the first and last clip
delta        end - start (signed)
max_step     the largest single-step change in the chain
steps        every per-step delta, in order, comma separated
uids         the ordered clip ids, comma separated
contiguous   whether every link is genuinely adjacent in the source
total_dur    summed duration of the clips, seconds
peak_start   strongest emotion of the first clip
peak_end     strongest emotion of the last clip
emit_frac    sampling weight (see below)

The file stores each chain once at the loosest setting (T = 0.25, cap = 0.25, mode = any, ecdfm normalisation); every tighter cell of the grid is a filter on delta, max_step and contiguous, so you can reproduce any row of any table in 7.5–7.7 with a pandas query. Emission is capped per bucket for size, and emit_frac records the sampling fraction so counts can be re-weighted; the exact counts are the ones in the tables above, which come from the full unsampled pass.

8 · How to use these files

In your home directory

corpus_stats.htmlthis document
norm_stats.jsonthe frozen normalisation constants — see below
norm_stats_README.mdprose explanation of the above
corpus_stats_deciles.parquetevery decile-bucket count in tidy form (scope, field, bucket, count)
corpus_stats_extremes.parquetper scope and field: n, p10, p90, counts above/below, |z|>2 counts
corpus_stats_bursts.parquetburst class counts per scope
corpus_stats_traj_grid.parquetevery trajectory grid cell (dataset × norm × mode × k × tier × cap × space)
trajectories_sample.parquet9,015-row readable sample of the mined trajectories, full schema

Under /e/data1/datasets/playground/mmlaion/schuhmann1/dramabox/traj2/ (bulk)

out/trajectories_v2.parquetthe full mined set, all chains, ~1 GB
stats/part1.json, part2.json, part3.jsonevery number on this page, machine readable
stats/globalhist.npzexact 4096-bin global histogram of all 105 fields
stats/partials/per-chunk accumulators; the pass is resumable from these
code/prescan → stats → statmerge → mine → traj3 → report

Applying norm_stats.json

It holds mean, std, n, min, max and a percentile ladder for all 105 numeric fields, at four addressing levels: global, per_dataset, per_language and per_dataset_language. Use it whenever you need a new batch of data — new shards, KartoffelPhon, a different corpus — to land on the same scale as everything measured here, without re-reading 130,785,282 rows.

import json
norm = json.load(open("norm_stats.json"))
s = norm["per_dataset"]["podcast"]["emo_Anger"]
z = (x - s["mean"]) / s["std"]            # z-score
u = (x - s["pct"]["p1"]) / (s["pct"]["p99"] - s["pct"]["p1"])   # robust 0-1

For the skewed emotion fields, prefer interpolating x against the pct ladder to get a percentile rather than using the z-score. Fall back per_dataset_language → per_dataset → global, and always record which level you used — z-scores from different levels are not comparable.

Querying the trajectories

import pandas as pd
t = pd.read_parquet(".../traj2/out/trajectories_v2.parquet")
# smooth 5-clip emotional ramps, strong tier, genuinely adjacent clips
sel = t[(t.space == "emo") & (t.k == 5) & (t.delta.abs() >= 0.50)
        & (t.max_step <= 0.20) & t.contiguous]

9 · What is not established

  • Nothing here was checked by ear. Every number describes what the annotator models emitted. If Empathic Insight systematically confuses Awe with silence, this document faithfully reports that confusion as data.
  • Burst class counts are utterance counts, not event counts (§6), and the rarest classes have single-digit support — those are as likely to be detector noise as real sounds.
  • Speaker identity is a proxy in five of the six datasets mined (§7.2); only MLS trajectories are certainly one human. CommonVoice and KartoffelPhon carry no usable speaker identity at all and are excluded from Part 3.
  • Contiguity is unmeasurable in podcast, snippets and evasnippets; their contiguous counts are near zero for that reason, not because the clips are non-adjacent.
  • Language effects are confounded with dataset (§5.5).
  • EuroSpeech is ~25 shards short of complete, and KartoffelPhon has no speaker labels, so it appears in Parts 1–2 but contributes nothing to Part 3 (§3). Neither is a large effect, but neither is zero.
  • Percentiles are histogram estimates to within one bin of 4096; means, standard deviations, minima, maxima and all counts are exact.
  • The trajectory language mix and "what moves" tables are estimated from a capped sample; all headline trajectory counts are exact.
  • No audio was built. If chains are rendered to audio later, the internal-silence defect documented in the earlier collage work applies and the fix in vc4arm/code/prep.py::collapse_internal (collapse >400 ms internal quiet to 150 ms with a 40 ms equal-power crossfade) must be used.
